title: How to choose a B2B help desk or support platform
summary: Most help desks were built for one person filing one ticket. B2B support looks different. Here's what to look for, what to skip, and how to decide in two weeks.
body_markdown:
> **The short version:** Most help desks were built for one person filing one ticket. B2B support is different. You're helping whole companies, and the hard questions need account context: who the customer is, what they pay for, what changed, and what engineering already knows. So pick a full help desk that thinks in accounts instead of tickets, has AI that answers the simple questions and investigates the complex ones with that context, connects to the tools your team already uses, covers every channel your customers use in one queue, and has a price that stays sane as you grow.


Picture a support lead at a growing B2B software company. It's Monday morning.


There's a help desk tab open with 40 new tickets. There's Slack, with 12 shared customer channels lit up. There's a spreadsheet tracking which accounts are up for renewal. And there's a Jira board where a bug from last week is still sitting.


None of these talk to each other. So the support lead becomes the glue.


If that sounds familiar, you probably don't need a "better ticketing tool." You need a support platform built for how B2B actually works. This guide is how we'd pick one.


## Why B2B support is different


A lot of help desks were designed for consumer support. One person has one problem, files one ticket, and gets one answer. That model works great for returns and password resets.


B2B is messier, in a few specific ways:


- **Your customer is a company.** One account might have an admin, three engineers, and an exec sponsor, all asking questions in different places.
- **The stakes are bigger.** A slow reply isn't just one unhappy user. It can show up in a renewal conversation six months later.
- **Customers don't want to fill out forms.** They want to message you in the shared Slack channel you set up during the deal, or in Microsoft Teams, or by email with their whole team cc'd.
- **The hard questions go deep.** "Why did this sync fail?" often means checking logs, looping in engineering, and filing a bug.
- **Support isn't the only team that cares.** Customer success, sales, and product all want to know what's going on with an account.


So when you compare tools, compare them against this reality. Not against a feature checklist from 2015.


## Traditional help desk vs. a modern B2B support platform


Here's the simplest way we can put the difference.


Traditional help desk Modern B2B support platform


Main unit of work A ticket An account, with tickets inside it


Where customers reach you Email and a web form Slack, Microsoft Teams, email, chat, portal, and more, in one inbox


Context on a new ticket The ticket itself Plan, history, open bugs, past calls, and who owns the account


AI Suggested replies and a help center bot Agents that investigate, take action, and hand off with a summary


Who uses it Support Support, customer success, and product


How it's priced Often per seat, plus per resolution for AI Varies, so check how cost grows with volume


A traditional help desk isn't bad. It's just built for a different job. If most of your customers are companies, you'll feel the gap fast.


## What to look for, one question at a time


Take these questions into every demo. Better yet, bring five real tickets from last month and ask each vendor to walk through them live.


### 1. Does it meet customers where they already are?


Ask which channels it supports today, not on the roadmap.


For most B2B teams, that means shared Slack channels, Microsoft Teams, email, and a chat widget. Some also need Discord, WhatsApp, a customer portal, or phone.


Then ask the follow-up: do all of those land in one queue, with the same SLAs and reports? Or is Slack a separate bolt-on with its own rules?


If your customers mostly live in shared channels, we wrote a whole post on[Slack-first support for B2B teams](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/slack-first-b2b-support) .


### 2. Does it think in accounts, not just tickets?


When a ticket comes in, can your team see who this customer is right away? Their plan, their recent tickets, any open bugs, and who their CSM is?


If your team has to open three other tools to answer "is this a big account?", that's time lost on every single ticket.


### 3. Does it connect to the rest of your stack?


Support doesn't live alone. Ask how it works with your CRM, your issue tracker, your call recorder, and your data warehouse.


The good version: filing a bug from a ticket takes one click, and the ticket updates when engineering ships the fix. The bad version: someone copies and pastes between tabs all day.


### 4. Can it handle SLAs and routing without a spreadsheet?


As you grow, you'll want different response times for different plans. You'll want the right ticket to reach the right person, fast.


Ask to see how SLAs and routing are set up. Ask what happens at 6 PM on a Friday when a message lands in a channel nobody's watching.


### 5. Does the AI actually do work?


Almost every tool has AI now. The question is what kind.


A chatbot answers simple questions from your help center. An agent can look up the account, check your systems, take action, and hand your team a clear summary when it needs a person. We break this down in[agentic support vs AI chatbots](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/agentic-support-vs-chatbots) .


If AI is a big part of your decision, use our[checklist for evaluating agentic support platforms](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/how-to-evaluate-agentic-support-platforms) . It goes deeper than we can here.


### 6. Does it help teams beyond support?


The same customer context that helps support helps everyone else, too.


Customer success wants early warning on at-risk accounts. Product wants to know which bugs and feature requests keep coming up. Sales wants a quick read on an account before a call.


If the platform can serve those teams, you get a lot more value from one tool.


### 7. How does the price grow with you?


Do the math with your real numbers. Take your monthly ticket volume, then double it. What does the bill look like at both numbers?


Watch out for pricing that climbs every time a customer writes in. That can make a busy month, or a big launch, surprisingly expensive.


### 8. Can you trust it with customer data?


Ask the boring questions early. SOC 2 Type II? Data residency options if you need EU hosting? Single sign-on? Audit logs?


If a vendor gets vague here, that tells you something.


### 9. How hard is it to switch?


Ask how migration works. Can they bring over your past tickets and knowledge base? How long does setup take for a team your size? Who helps you through it?


A great tool you can't move into is not a great tool.


## A note for product-led B2B teams


Product-led companies have a twist. You might have thousands of self-serve users who want quick answers in a chat widget, plus a few hundred big accounts who expect a shared Slack channel and a named person.


That's two very different support styles. Look for a platform that handles both in one place, so you're not running two help desks and two sets of reports.


Some teams take this even further and support both business and consumer customers side by side. Sardine and Wispr Flow are two examples of companies doing that on Pylon.


## Red flags to watch for in a demo


A few things that should make you pause:


- **"Slack support" means a notification bot.** Messages get forwarded somewhere, but replies don't flow back into the customer's channel.
- **Every account looks the same.** No plan, no ARR, no history next to the ticket.
- **The AI only answers from your help center.** That's fine for easy questions. It won't help much with the hard ones.
- **Every change needs the vendor.** If your team can't update workflows or AI instructions themselves, it'll fall behind your product fast.
- **The pricing page doesn't add up.** If you can't predict next year's bill, that's a problem.


## How to make the decision in two weeks


You don't need a three-month process. Here's a simple one.


1. **Write down your top five pains.** Missed Slack messages, no account context, slow bug handoffs, whatever is actually hurting.
2. **Pull five real tickets.** Pick the ones that took your team the longest last month.
3. **Shortlist two or three tools.** More than that and the demos blur together.
4. **Run the same tickets through each one.** Score each tool from 1 to 5 on the questions above.
5. **Do the pricing math.** Today's volume, and double it.
6. **Talk to a customer who looks like you.** Same size, same channels, same kind of product.


Pick the one that handled your tickets best. Not the one with the slickest demo.

## FAQ


### What should a B2B SaaS company look for in a help desk?


Look for a full help desk built around accounts, not single tickets. It should show account context on every ticket, have AI that answers simple questions and investigates complex ones with that context, connect to your CRM and issue tracker, and handle SLAs and routing. It should also cover the channels your customers already use, like email, chat, Slack, and Microsoft Teams, in one queue. Pricing should stay predictable as volume grows.


### What's the difference between a traditional help desk and a B2B support platform?


A traditional help desk is built around single tickets, usually from email and web forms. A B2B support platform is built around accounts. It brings every channel into one inbox and gives your team the customer's full context while they work.


### Should B2B teams choose a traditional help desk or Slack-first support?


If many of your customers already talk to you in shared Slack or Microsoft Teams channels, choose a platform that treats those channels as first-class. The best options handle Slack and Teams and also email, chat, and other channels in one queue, so you're not stuck choosing.


### What's the best support platform for a product-led B2B company?


Look for one that can handle lots of self-serve users and high-touch enterprise accounts in one place. That usually means chat and email for smaller users, shared channels for big accounts, and one set of SLAs and reports across both.


### How long should it take to choose a support platform?


About two weeks is usually enough. Shortlist two or three tools, run the same real tickets through each, do the pricing math at today's volume and double it, and talk to a customer that looks like you.


### Is Pylon an add-on for Zendesk or Intercom?


No. Pylon is the help desk itself: ticketing, SLAs, routing, knowledge base, every channel, and AI agents with account context, in one B2B support platform. Teams move to Pylon to replace their help desk, not to bolt AI onto an existing one.
